---
title: "Charts: scaling data to pixels"
---

A chart is a pile of rectangles that happens to mean something. You can already
put a rectangle into an SVG from TypeScript, so what is missing is the
arithmetic between the numbers you have and the pixels the picture has. That
arithmetic is the whole job. Start by getting it wrong on purpose.

## Four bars hanging from the ceiling {#sec-charts-hanging}

1. Create a new app `chart-experiment` from our template inside `coursework/`.
2. In `index.html`, replace everything between `<body>` and `</body>` with
   this:

   ```html
   <h1>Four bars</h1>
   <svg id="chart" viewBox="0 0 400 300" width="400" height="300" role="img" aria-label="Four bars"></svg>
   <script src="./src/index.ts" type="module"></script>
   ```

3. Replace the two lines in `src/index.ts` with this:

   ```ts
   const SVG_NS = 'http://www.w3.org/2000/svg';

   const chart = document.querySelector<SVGSVGElement>('#chart');

   if (!chart) {
     throw new Error('The chart is missing');
   }

   const values = [12, 40, 25, 60];

   for (let i = 0; i < values.length; i++) {
     const value = values[i];
     if (value === undefined) {
       continue;
     }

     const bar = document.createElementNS(SVG_NS, 'rect');
     bar.setAttribute('x', String(20 + i * 60));
     bar.setAttribute('y', '0');
     bar.setAttribute('width', '40');
     bar.setAttribute('height', String(value));
     bar.setAttribute('fill', 'seagreen');
     chart.append(bar);
   }
   ```

Four green bars, and every one of them hangs down from the top edge. The
biggest value gives the longest bar, so the data is in there, just upside down.
A rectangle's `y` is its **top** edge, and y counts downward from the top of
the picture.

## Stand them on the floor {#sec-charts-flip}

The floor of this picture is at y 300, the bottom of the `viewBox`, and a bar
that is `value` pixels tall has to start `value` pixels above it. Change the
`y` line:

```ts
bar.setAttribute('y', String(300 - value));
```

Now the bars grow upward from the bottom. Every chart you write does that
subtraction somewhere, and forgetting it is the usual reason a chart comes out
hanging from the ceiling.

## The bar that runs off the picture {#sec-charts-overflow}

Change the last value in the array from `60` to `420` and look again. Its `y`
came out as -120, so the bar is cut off at the top edge and dwarfs the others.

Nothing is broken. The data goes up to 420 while the picture is 300 pixels
tall, and the code treated one value as one pixel. Values and pixels are two
different scales, and the code has to convert between them the way you convert
euros to dollars.

## One function turns values into pixels {#sec-charts-scale}

Give the drawing a frame first. The plot keeps a margin around itself so there
is room for the axis and its labels, and each distance gets a name instead of
being sprinkled through the code. Put this above the loop:

```ts
const MARGIN = 40;
const CHART_WIDTH = 320;
const CHART_HEIGHT = 220;
const BASELINE = MARGIN + CHART_HEIGHT;
const MIN_VALUE = 0;
const MAX_VALUE = 500;
```

`BASELINE` is the y of the floor, 260. Above it sit 220 pixels of plot, and the
values in there run from 0 to 500. One arrow function maps the one range onto
the other:

```ts
const scaleY = (value: number) => BASELINE - ((value - MIN_VALUE) / (MAX_VALUE - MIN_VALUE)) * CHART_HEIGHT;
```

Read it in three moves. `(value - MIN_VALUE) / (MAX_VALUE - MIN_VALUE)` asks how
far up the range the value sits and answers with a share between 0 and 1.
Multiplying by `CHART_HEIGHT` turns that share into pixels. Subtracting from
`BASELINE` does the flip you just did by hand. Try 250: half the range, so 110
pixels, so 260 - 110 = 150, halfway up the plot.

Now let the loop use it. Change the array to
`const values = [120, 400, 250, 480];` and replace the body of the loop:

```ts
const BAR_WIDTH = 40;
const slotWidth = CHART_WIDTH / values.length;

for (let i = 0; i < values.length; i++) {
  const value = values[i];
  if (value === undefined) {
    continue;
  }

  const top = scaleY(value);
  const centerX = MARGIN + i * slotWidth + slotWidth / 2;

  const bar = document.createElementNS(SVG_NS, 'rect');
  bar.setAttribute('x', String(centerX - BAR_WIDTH / 2));
  bar.setAttribute('y', String(top));
  bar.setAttribute('width', String(BAR_WIDTH));
  bar.setAttribute('height', String(BASELINE - top));
  bar.setAttribute('fill', 'seagreen');
  chart.append(bar);
}
```

Every bar fits now, and each one gets a slot of equal width and sits in the
middle of it, so changing `BAR_WIDTH` changes the gaps and nothing else. Raise
`MAX_VALUE` to 1000 and the whole chart shrinks to half height without one
other edit. That is what naming the numbers buys you.

## Axes, ticks, and labels {#sec-charts-axes}

An axis is a `line`, and so is a tick. A tick label is a `text`. Those parts
belong together, so put them in one `g` element and give the group the
attributes they share:

```ts
const axes = document.createElementNS(SVG_NS, 'g');
axes.setAttribute('stroke', '#333');

const yAxis = document.createElementNS(SVG_NS, 'line');
yAxis.setAttribute('x1', String(MARGIN));
yAxis.setAttribute('y1', String(MARGIN));
yAxis.setAttribute('x2', String(MARGIN));
yAxis.setAttribute('y2', String(BASELINE));
axes.append(yAxis);

const xAxis = document.createElementNS(SVG_NS, 'line');
xAxis.setAttribute('x1', String(MARGIN));
xAxis.setAttribute('y1', String(BASELINE));
xAxis.setAttribute('x2', String(MARGIN + CHART_WIDTH));
xAxis.setAttribute('y2', String(BASELINE));
axes.append(xAxis);
```

Put that block above the loop that draws the bars, because SVG paints in
document order and whatever is appended last lies on top. A `g` hands its
attributes down to everything inside it, so one `stroke` colors both lines.

The ticks come out of a loop over values, not over pixels, because `scaleY`
already knows where a value lives:

```ts
for (let value = MIN_VALUE; value <= MAX_VALUE; value += 100) {
  const y = scaleY(value);

  const tick = document.createElementNS(SVG_NS, 'line');
  tick.setAttribute('x1', String(MARGIN - 6));
  tick.setAttribute('y1', String(y));
  tick.setAttribute('x2', String(MARGIN));
  tick.setAttribute('y2', String(y));
  axes.append(tick);

  const label = document.createElementNS(SVG_NS, 'text');
  label.setAttribute('x', String(MARGIN - 12));
  label.setAttribute('y', String(y));
  label.setAttribute('font-size', '12');
  label.setAttribute('fill', '#333');
  label.setAttribute('stroke', 'none');
  label.textContent = String(value);
  axes.append(label);
}

chart.append(axes);
```

The `stroke="none"` is there because the group's stroke would otherwise outline
every letter. And the numbers land wrong twice over: each one starts at its own
x and runs right across the axis, and it rests its bottom edge on the tick
instead of straddling it. `text-anchor`, which you already used when writing
SVG by hand, takes care of the horizontal half, a second attribute takes the
vertical one, and the research box below sends you after the exact values.

## Redraw means clear and rebuild {#sec-charts-redraw}

A chart that reacts to a form has to change. Do not go hunting for the one
`rect` whose height is now wrong. Throw the drawing away and build it again
from the data. Picture what you wrote above wrapped into two helpers,
`drawAxes` and `drawBars`. Then the whole update is three lines:

```ts
const drawChart = () => {
  plot.replaceChildren();
  drawAxes();
  drawBars();
};
```

`replaceChildren()` with no arguments empties an element. Call it on the `<svg>`
itself and it takes everything, including whatever you drew by hand in the
HTML, so give the moving parts their own layer: a `<g id="plot"></g>` that your
code clears, with anything permanent sitting outside it. You do not need to
rebuild the experiment this way; the bubble chart below is where the pattern
goes to work.

The `role="img"` and `aria-label` on the `<svg>` tell a screen reader what the
picture shows, and Biome's accessibility rules insist on them. Being attributes
on the element itself, they survive every redraw.

::: {.research title="Where does a text sit, and what makes a line dashed?"}
The first chart you build below writes a number next to every tick, a month
under every bar, a value that pops up when the mouse rests on a bar, and a
dashed line across the plot. The code above does none of those four things.

1. A tick label should stop just left of its tick and sit level with it. Which
   value of `text-anchor` makes a text **end** at its `x` instead of starting
   there? And which second attribute places a text up and down on its `y`, with
   which value for centering it on the point?
2. SVG has a `<title>` element, and one place to put it is inside a single
   shape, as a child of a `rect` or a `circle`. What does the browser then do
   with that text, and when does the user get to see it?
3. Which attribute turns a solid SVG line into a dashed one, and what do the
   numbers you hand it mean?

Question 1 is exam material. A chart whose labels are half a centimeter off is
a chart you have to repair without internet and without AI.
:::

## Exercise A: a year of energy {#sec-charts-bar-exercise}

Twelve monthly readings, twelve bars, and a dashed line where the budget ends.
Every bar above that line turns red.

{{< exercise bar-chart >}}

1. Create the app inside `coursework/` of your course repository as the box
   above says, then read `index.html`: it holds an `<svg id="chart">` of 640
   by 400 and an empty `<p id="legend">` under it.
2. In `src/index.ts`, replace everything with `import './styles.css';` and
   `const SVG_NS = 'http://www.w3.org/2000/svg';`, then look up `#chart` as
   `SVGSVGElement` and `#legend` as `HTMLParagraphElement` and throw if either
   is missing. Run `npm start`. You get a heading and an empty frame, and a
   clean console.
3. Take over the data and the layout:

   ```ts
   const MARGIN_LEFT = 60;
   const MARGIN_TOP = 30;
   const CHART_WIDTH = 540;
   const CHART_HEIGHT = 300;
   const BASELINE = MARGIN_TOP + CHART_HEIGHT;
   const BAR_WIDTH = 30;
   const MIN_VALUE = 0;
   const MAX_VALUE = 80;
   const TICK_STEP = 20;
   const THRESHOLD = 50;

   const MONTHS = ['Jan', 'Feb', 'Mar', 'Apr', 'May', 'Jun', 'Jul', 'Aug', 'Sep', 'Oct', 'Nov', 'Dec'];
   const values = [62, 58, 47, 39, 28, 21, 18, 20, 27, 41, 55, 68];
   ```

   The numbers are kilowatt hours, one per month.
4. Write `scaleY` for these constants, the same shape as the one in this
   chapter. Check it before you run it: `scaleY(0)` must be 330 and `scaleY(80)`
   must be 30.
5. Draw the axes into a `g` element with the CSS class `axis`, which the
   stylesheet already colors. The y axis runs from `MARGIN_TOP` down to
   `BASELINE` at x `MARGIN_LEFT`, the x axis from `MARGIN_LEFT` to
   `MARGIN_LEFT + CHART_WIDTH` at y `BASELINE`. Expected result: a large L in
   the frame.
6. Loop from `MIN_VALUE` to `MAX_VALUE` in steps of `TICK_STEP`. Give every
   value a short tick left of the y axis and a `text` with the number and the
   class `label`, ending just before the tick and centered on it. The research
   box names the two attributes. Expected result: 0, 20, 40, 60, and 80 stand
   in a tidy column.
7. Draw the twelve bars. Each bar gets the class `bar`, its slot is
   `CHART_WIDTH / values.length` wide, and the bar sits centered in its slot
   with the width `BAR_WIDTH`. A bar whose value is greater than `THRESHOLD`
   gets the extra class `over`. Expected result: eight green bars and four red
   ones for January, February, November, and December.
8. Draw the threshold line: one dashed `line` with the class `threshold`,
   running the full width of the plot at `scaleY(THRESHOLD)`. The research box
   names the attribute for the dashes.
9. Write the month name under each bar as a `text` with the class `label`,
   centered on the same slot middle as the bar, about 18 pixels below
   `BASELINE`.
10. Let every bar say its own number. Append a `title` element to the `rect`
    itself, with text such as `Nov: 55 kWh`. Expected result: rest the mouse on
    a bar for a second and a small box shows that text.
11. Fill the legend. Count the months above `THRESHOLD` with a loop and write
    a sentence such as `4 of 12 months are above 50 kWh.` into `#legend`.
12. Run `npm run check` and fix what Biome reports.

Change one number in `values` to 200 and reload: the bar shoots out of the top.
Raise `MAX_VALUE` to 200 and the chart is right again, tick labels and all,
because every pixel in it came out of `scaleY`.

## Exercise B: the bubble chart {#sec-charts-bubble-exercise}

Now the data comes from the user. A form with a color picker, two number
fields, and a slider adds one bubble at a time to a coordinate system that runs
from 0 to 100 in both directions. This is a rebuilt version of a real exam, and
steps 3 to 9 are the must-have set: read the form, refuse values outside the
range with a visible message, put the circle in the right place, and clear the
chart on demand. Step 10 is the finishing touch.

{{< exercise bubble-chart >}}

1. Create the app inside `coursework/` of your course repository as the box
   above says, then read `index.html`. The chart area is drawn by hand inside
   a `<g class="axis">`: a square from (50, 50) to (450, 450) in SVG pixels,
   with nine ticks per axis. Below it sits an empty `<g id="bubbleLayer">`,
   the layer your code owns.
2. In `src/index.ts`, replace everything with the stylesheet import and
   `SVG_NS`, then look up `#bubbleForm`, `#bubbleColor`, `#bubbleX`,
   `#bubbleY`, `#bubbleSize`, `#sizeValue`, `#bubbleError`, `#clearBubbles`,
   and `#bubbleLayer` as an `SVGGElement`. One `if` that throws covers all
   nine. Run `npm start`: the form and the empty chart area appear.
3. Add the layout constants `MARGIN` 50, `AXIS_LENGTH` 400, `BASELINE`
   `MARGIN + AXIS_LENGTH`, `MIN_VALUE` 0, and `MAX_VALUE` 100. Write `scaleX`,
   which maps a value to a pixel from left to right, and `scaleY`, which maps
   it from bottom to top. Check: `scaleX(0)` is 50, `scaleX(100)` is 450,
   `scaleY(0)` is 450, and `scaleY(100)` is 50.
4. Describe one bubble with a compound type and keep a list of them:

   ```ts
   type Bubble = {
     x: number;
     y: number;
     size: number;
     color: string;
   };

   let bubbles: Bubble[] = [];
   ```

5. Write `const drawBubbles = () => { ... };`. It clears the bubble layer with
   `replaceChildren()` and loops over `bubbles` with `for...of`, creating one
   `circle` per entry: `cx` from `scaleX`, `cy` from `scaleY`, `r` from the
   size, and `fill` from the color.
6. Listen for `submit` on the form with `event.preventDefault()` as the first
   line. Read x, y, and the size with `valueAsNumber`, the color with `value`.
7. Refuse bad coordinates. When x or y is `NaN`, below `MIN_VALUE`, or above
   `MAX_VALUE`, write a message such as `Please enter an x and a y between 0 and
   100.` into `#bubbleError`, put the cursor back with `focus()`, and `return`.
   Expected result: typing 150 into the x field and pressing Enter shows the
   message and draws nothing.
8. In the good case, clear the error text, `push` a new object
   `{ x, y, size, color }` onto `bubbles`, and call `drawBubbles()`. Expected
   result: x 0 and y 0 puts a circle in the lower left corner, x 100 and y 100
   in the upper right, and x 50 with y 50 in the middle.
9. Make the **Clear** button empty the array, clear the error text, and redraw.
   Assigning a fresh `[]` to `bubbles` is the shortest way to empty it.
   Expected result: the circles are gone and the hand-drawn axes are still
   there, because your code only ever clears the `#bubbleLayer` group.
10. Show the slider's number: listen for `input` on the range field and write
    its `value` into the `#sizeValue` span, so the label counts along as you
    drag.
11. Run `npm run check` and fix what Biome reports.

Add half a dozen bubbles and look at what your code did. No circle was ever
edited after it was created. The array holds the truth and the picture is a
copy of it, so every change goes to the array first and the drawing follows. A
chart that later has to remove a bubble costs you two more lines that way.

::: {.callout-tip}
## Bonus: keep the bubble inside the box

A bubble at x 100 with size 50 sticks half out of the chart area. Refuse it:
the circle fits when `scaleX(x) - size` is at least `MARGIN` and
`scaleX(x) + size` is at most `MARGIN + AXIS_LENGTH`, and the same check with
`scaleY(y)` for the vertical direction.
:::
